teaser.text: Micron Technology makes the memory chips and storage devices that computers use to work and keep data. It sells different products because a device needs different kinds of memory for different jobs.

dividend.title: Micron dividend
dividend.meta_description: Micron pays $0.15 quarterly; fiscal 2026 real free cash flow after stock pay was $57,681 million, with the memo tracking yield and risks.
dividend.opening: Micron pays $0.15 per share quarterly, or $0.60 per share, and its real free cash flow after stock pay reached $57,681 million in fiscal 2026. That cash covered the dividend, while Micron says capital returns will increase but has not set a dividend target.
dividend.closing: The full memo also covers Micron’s business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: How much does Micron pay per share?

paragraphs.text: The dividend starts at $0.60 per share because the declared quarterly rate is $0.15. The base case raises it gradually to $0.96 by FY2030. The bear case freezes it at $0.60, while the bull case reaches $1.50 as excess cash expands. Micron has said capital returns will increase, but has not set a dividend target.

blocks.heading: Does Micron’s cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: FY2026 reversed the pressure. Real free cash flow reached $57,681 million. Micron repaid $10,043 million of debt, including finance-lease principal, and distributions to shareholders became a small share of the year’s cash generation. The repurchase total included employee tax withholding, so it should not be treated as identical to market buybacks.

blocks.heading: What is Micron’s dividend yield at its share price?

paragraphs.text: At $1,067.55 a share, investors value Micron’s equity at $1,205,683.66 million. Enterprise value, which values the operating business after cash and borrowings, is $1,167,428.66 million. The difference implies $38,255 million of net cash, although some of that cash is restricted and may not be freely available.

earnings.opening: Micron's next results are expected on December 23, 2026. Watch whether Micron turns spending into profitable capacity while preserving enough cash for obligations and shareholder returns.
earnings.closing: The full memo also explains Micron's business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: What has Micron guided for fiscal 2027?

paragraphs.text: Guidance is management’s forecast of what it expects to deliver. Micron’s September 30 outlook covers revenue, earnings, margins, expenses and investment. It also reports non-GAAP earnings, which remove selected costs from standard accounting. That can make comparisons easier, but the excluded costs remain real costs.

blocks.heading: Did Micron keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: There is evidence of restraint and execution. During the downturn, Micron cut the CEO’s salary by 20% and executive vice presidents’ salaries by 15%. Later, the board certified strong achievement against earlier product goals. Those facts support management’s credibility, but they do not prove how much of the reward came from management rather than favorable industry prices.

blocks.heading: How have Micron's revenue and profit changed in the last eight quarters?

paragraphs.text: The rise continued across the year. Quarterly revenue increased from $13,643 million in November to $54,229 million in September. But September had 14 weeks, compared with 13 in May. Reported sequential revenue growth was about 30.8%; average weekly revenue growth was about 21.5%. The calendar explains part, not all, of the acceleration.

Cash offers a second check. Final-quarter operating cash was $43,973 million and capital spending was $11,110 million, leaving $32,863 million before incentives and equipment-sale proceeds. Net income reached $37,701 million, with diluted EPS of $32.87. Yet manufacturing-bonus costs sitting in inventory have not all reached gross margin.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Micron's next results?

paragraphs.text: The decisive evidence will be whether Micron turns spending into profitable capacity while preserving enough cash for obligations and shareholder returns.
